trivia_fact: The term "GitOps" was coined by Alexis Richardson, CEO of Weaveworks, in a 2017 blog post. He described it as an operating model where Git repositories serve as the single source of truth for both application code and infrastructure declarations.

GitOps uses Git as the single source of truth because Git already solves versioning, audit trails, rollback, and collaboration. The insight was that if Git is good enough to manage your code, it's good enough to manage your infrastructure state.

GitOps distinguishes between "pull" and "push" deployment models. In the pull model (preferred), an agent in the cluster watches the Git repo and applies changes automatically. In the push model, a CI pipeline pushes changes to the cluster. The pull model is considered more secure.

Argo CD was created at Intuit (the TurboTax company) in 2018 and donated to the CNCF. It became the most popular GitOps tool for Kubernetes, providing a declarative, Git-based continuous delivery engine with a visual UI for cluster state.

Flux was created by Weaveworks (the company that coined GitOps) and was one of the first GitOps implementations. Flux v2 was rewritten from scratch and graduated as a CNCF project. It pioneered the "reconciliation loop" pattern for GitOps controllers.

In a twist of irony, Weaveworks — the company that coined "GitOps" and built Flux — shut down in February 2024 due to financial difficulties. The GitOps concept they created outlived the company, with ArgoCD and Flux continuing under CNCF stewardship.

The GitOps reconciliation loop continuously compares the desired state in Git with the actual state in the cluster and corrects any drift. This concept was borrowed from Kubernetes' own controller pattern, where controllers constantly reconcile actual state toward desired state.

GitOps solves "configuration drift" — when environments silently deviate from their declared state due to manual changes. By continuously reconciling against Git, unauthorized changes are automatically reverted, providing both operational safety and compliance audit trails.

The OpenGitOps project (CNCF sandbox) formalized four GitOps principles in 2021: declarative configuration, versioned and immutable desired state, automatic pull-based reconciliation, and continuous reconciliation. These principles are vendor-neutral and tool-agnostic.

GitOps has been extended with "progressive delivery" tools like Argo Rollouts and Flagger, which add canary releases and blue-green deployments to the GitOps model. The desired state in Git includes rollout strategy, and the controller handles the gradual traffic shift.
